hook: A 50-user dashboard watching 100 live documents costs about $1,296 a month in Firestore reads and a flat $25 on Supabase Pro. Same screen, same users: the only thing that changed is what the vendor counts.

sections.title: The billing unit decides what code you may write
sections.content:
**Supabase sells a machine.** You rent compute, a disk and a connection ceiling, and Postgres does whatever fits inside them. **Firebase sells events.** Every document read, write, index batch and listener update is a line on the invoice.

What each philosophy forbids:

- **Firestore forbids JOINs.** Related data gets duplicated into documents or fetched with extra reads, and every extra read is billed.
- **Supabase forbids infinite concurrency.** The $10 Micro instance stops at 60 direct / 200 pooled connections. No tier on the price sheet sells an unlimited pool; XL tops out at 1,000.

Read the price list as a penalty table:

| Meter | Unit price | Pattern it punishes |
|---|---|---|
| Firestore reads | $0.03 / 100,000 | Live listeners on hot documents |
| Firestore writes | $0.09 / 100,000 | Per-keystroke saves, chatty counters |
| Supabase disk | $0.125/GB over 8 GB | Keeping everything forever |
| Supabase compute | $10 to $210 per project | Many connections, many projects |

sections.title: Firestore bills you for every minute a tab stays open
sections.content:
A listener is not a free subscription. Firestore bills a read each time a document enters or updates in a live listener's result set, and one more when a change pushes it out. The meter runs while nobody clicks.

Take 50 users, each watching 100 documents that change 20 times a minute:

```python
users, docs, changes_per_min = 50, 100, 20
reads = users * docs * changes_per_min * 60 * 24 * 30
print(reads)                   # 4.32B events, zero clicks
print(reads / 100_000 * 0.03)  # here it breaks: ~1296 dollars/month
```

The same shape on Supabase Pro with Micro compute is a flat $25/month. Reconnects make Firestore worse:

- Offline persistence **off**: every reconnect is billed like a brand-new query.
- Persistence **on** but disconnected for more than 30 minutes: same bill.

A laptop closed over lunch pays for its whole result set again at 13:00.

sections.title: Supabase swaps a metered risk for a capacity risk
sections.content:
Postgres Changes is a database event stream, and you opt in per table:

```sql
-- opt-in per table: unlisted tables never stream
alter publication supabase_realtime add table your_table_name;
```

That stream has no per-read meter. The ceiling is the instance: its connection limits and its compute tier.

| Compute | Price | Direct / pooled |
|---|---|---|
| Micro | $10 | 60 / 200 |
| Small | $15 | 90 / 400 |
| Medium | $60 | 120 / 600 |
| Large | $110 | 160 / 800 |
| XL | $210 | 240 / 1,000 |

> You stop paying for surprise. You start paying for headroom.

Firestore fails as a large invoice. Supabase fails as a refused connection in your busiest hour, and the fix is a tier upgrade, not a config flag. Size for peak, not average.

sections.title: Index entry reads are the Firestore line item nobody quotes
sections.content:
Document reads get the attention. Index entry reads sit underneath them:

- One read per batch of up to 1,000 index entries a query reads.
- A query with **one** range field pays nothing for index entries. Add a second range field and billing starts.
- `count()`, `sum()` and `avg()` bill index reads, with a 1-document-read minimum even at zero entries.

Firestore's own docs give the example: `count()` over 1,500 index entries bills 2 document reads. Cheap per call. Now put that count in a page header that every open listener refreshes.

> Every filter you add is a pricing decision, not just a schema decision.

Audit any query that combines two range fields before it ships.

sections.title: Migration is a schema project with a script attached
sections.content:
`supabase-community/firebase-to-supabase` on GitHub is community tooling, not an official CLI. What it does:

1. `firestore2json.js` exports a collection; `json2supabase.js` loads it into a table. One collection, one table.
2. Fields are flattened to `text`, `numeric`, `boolean` or `jsonb`.
3. Splitting nested JSON into related tables needs custom hooks you write.

The schema design Firestore let you skip lands on your desk now.

Auth is the sharper edge. `firestoreusers2json` and `import_users` move users, importing hashes with Firestore's SCRYPT parameters (`base64_signer_key`, `base64_salt_separator`, `rounds`, `mem_cost`).

> Verifying an existing Firebase password on first login needs a middleware the repo itself marks **work in progress**. The AWS Lambda variant is listed as TBD.

Budget a forced password reset as the fallback.

sections.title: Pick Supabase if users watch; keep Firestore if they mostly don't
sections.content:
**If your product keeps live listeners open on documents that change every minute, Supabase wins**: its bill tracks the machine, not the watching. If your app fits Firestore's daily free quota of 50,000 reads and 20,000 writes, moving buys schema work, not savings.

Check today, in this order:

1. Multiply listeners × documents per listener × changes per minute × (60 × 24 × 30) minutes, then × $0.03 per 100,000.
2. Find every hot-path query with two range fields or a `count()`.
3. On Supabase, compare peak concurrent connections to Micro's 60 direct / 200 pooled.
4. Decide whether your users can survive a password reset.

decision_matrix.situation: Live dashboard: many users watching documents that change every minute
decision_matrix.why: Firestore bills a read per listener update, so cost scales with users × documents × changes, while Supabase bills a flat compute tier.

decision_matrix.situation: Quiet app that fits inside Firestore's daily free quota
decision_matrix.why: At 50,000 free reads a day there is no bill to cut, and migration adds schema work.

decision_matrix.situation: Relational data with reporting queries across entities
decision_matrix.why: Firestore has no JOINs, so every relation becomes duplicated data or extra billed reads.

decision_matrix.situation: Mobile users who go offline and reconnect often
decision_matrix.pick: Supabase, or Firestore with offline persistence on
decision_matrix.why: With persistence off, every Firestore reconnect is billed like a brand-new query.

decision_matrix.situation: Spiky concurrency far beyond a few hundred connections, small budget
decision_matrix.why: Supabase's pooled ceiling runs from 200 on Micro to 1,000 on XL at $210 compute, while Firestore meters events, not connections.

decision_matrix.situation: Agency running many small client projects
decision_matrix.pick: Firestore, unless each client pays for compute
decision_matrix.why: Every extra Supabase project adds its own compute line, $10 for each Micro.

decision_matrix.situation: Large Firebase Auth user base with passwords, no tolerance for resets
decision_matrix.pick: Neither — stay put until the auth middleware ships
decision_matrix.why: First-login verification of Firebase passwords depends on middleware the migration repo marks work in progress.

decision_matrix.situation: Aggregate counts shown on hot, frequently refreshed pages
decision_matrix.why: Firestore's count() bills index reads on every call, with a 1-document-read minimum.

cost_math.label: Firestore: 50-user live dashboard (derived from fact-sheet rates)
Supabase Pro: same dashboard on one Micro project
Supabase's official billing example: Pro org, 2 Micro projects

verdict_summary: Supabase wins if your app keeps live listeners open on frequently changing data: that dashboard shape costs ≈ $1,296/month in Firestore reads against a flat $25 on Supabase Pro. Firestore wins if your app is quiet enough to live inside its daily free quota and never needs a JOIN, because leaving means hand-written schema hooks and an unfinished password-verification middleware.

faqs.q: Can I park a Supabase Free project for a demo that sits idle?
faqs.a: Not reliably: Free projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity, and Free allows only 2 active projects. Pro projects are never paused for inactivity.

faqs.q: Does offset pagination save reads on Firestore?
faqs.a: No. Firestore bills a read for every skipped document, so offset 10 returning 1 document costs 11 reads.

faqs.q: Will Supabase Realtime leak rows a user shouldn't see?
faqs.a: Postgres Changes subscriptions are RLS-aware, so clients receive only rows they are allowed to select. Supabase's docs also document Broadcast as an alternative way to subscribe to database changes.

faqs.q: How is Firestore vector search billed?
faqs.a: kNN vector search bills one read per batch of up to 100 vector index entries. That is a tenth of the 1,000-entry batch size used for regular index entry reads.
